analysis.one_liner: Offers an elective simplified income tax, repeals the estate tax, and cuts corporate and investment tax rates.
analysis.headline: Introduced on January 5, 2011 with 2 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill lets taxpayers elect a simplified income tax with three rates (10%, 15%, and 30%), eliminates the estate and gift tax entirely, cuts the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%, drops the capital gains and dividend rate from 15% to 10%, and adjusts the value of assets for inflation before taxing gains on sales. It also creates new tax-exempt savings accounts for retirement, general savings, and job training, permanently fixes the alternative minimum tax exemption, expands the medical expense deduction for people under 65 without employer coverage, makes the research tax credit permanent, and makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest benefits go to the wealthiest households: the estate tax repeal means the largest estates pay nothing, the 10% capital gains rate and inflation-indexed asset basis sharply cut taxes on investment gains, and the 25% corporate rate cuts taxes on profitable corporations. Corporations and universities that claim the research credit gain a permanent benefit. Banks and brokerages gain as administrators of the new retirement, lifetime savings, and lifetime skills accounts. Modest gains flow to a narrower group: middle-income filers who elect the simplified tax, taxpayers whose incomes put them near the alternative minimum tax, and people under 65 without employer health coverage who pay large out-of-pocket medical costs.

how_it_helps.text: The elective system taxes the first $40,000 of simplified taxable income at 10%, the next $110,000 at 15%, and amounts above $150,000 at 30%, keeping only the mortgage interest, state income tax, charitable, and limited medical deductions [S3].
The bill repeals the estate and gift tax for decedents dying and gifts made after 2010 [S2][S3].
It lowers the maximum corporate rate to 25% and the maximum capital gains and dividend rate to 10% [S2][S3].

For assets held more than three years, the bill increases an owner's basis by inflation (measured by the GDP deflator) before computing gain, so part of every long-held asset's sale gain goes untaxed [S3].
It makes the alternative minimum tax exemption amounts permanent and indexes them for inflation [S2][S3].

It allows people under 65 without employer coverage to deduct up to $7,500 per person ($15,000 per taxpayer) in medical expenses with no income threshold, with unused room convertible into health savings account contributions, and lets health savings accounts pass to any designated beneficiary at death [S3].
It makes the research credit permanent and makes permanent the tax provisions of the 2001 and 2003 tax laws that were scheduled to expire [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions, so the federal treasury absorbs the cost of the estate tax repeal, the rate cuts, and the inflation indexing — meaning either larger deficits or offsetting cuts and tax shifts elsewhere. Taxpayers who elect the simplified system give up most deductions and credits (keeping only mortgage interest, state income taxes, charitable gifts, and limited medical expenses), which can raise taxes for filers who rely on itemized deductions, child credits beyond the child tax credit, or other benefits. Repealing the estate tax shifts the tax burden toward wage earners whose income is taxed at ordinary rates.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and gift tax removes the only federal tax on very large inheritances, benefiting a small number of the largest estates while removing revenue [S2][S3].

The simplified tax strips away most deductions and credits — no standard deduction, no earned income credit, no education or energy credits, and no deduction for property or general sales taxes — so some filers who elect it would pay more than under current law [S3].

Indexing asset basis for inflation plus a 10% capital gains rate would substantially shrink the tax on investment gains relative to wage income, and the bill text includes no revenue offsets for any of its tax cuts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real, if modest, help for specific groups — middle-income filers who elect the simplified rate structure, taxpayers near the AMT, and uninsured people under 65 facing large medical bills — and genuine simplification. But the largest and most permanent changes (full estate tax repeal, a 10% capital gains rate, inflation-indexed basis, and a 25% corporate rate) concentrate their value at the top of the wealth distribution and on corporate profits, with no identified funding source. As drafted, the distribution of benefits skews heavily toward those already holding substantial assets, and the simplified option's deduction tradeoffs mean it is not uniformly a tax cut even for middle-income filers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 112th Congress ended without ever coming to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Dreier introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the first day of the 112th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Two House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the estate tax, the 15% capital gains rate, and the 35% corporate rate stayed in place, so the federal treasury kept that revenue and large estates and investors remained subject to existing tax. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing either — the AMT fix, the medical deduction expansion, and the simplified option never became law — leaving the existing tax code in place for everyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury kept current tax law; no changes

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans sponsored the bill (the sponsor plus 2 Republican cosponsors), and no votes were ever taken, so no record of broader party support or opposition exists.

industries.note: Estate tax repeal, a 10% capital gains rate, and inflation-indexed basis deliver the bill's largest dollar benefits to the wealthiest families. The revenue loss has no offset in the bill, so the cost would fall on other taxpayers or the deficit.

Cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 25% and making the research credit permanent lowers taxes on profitable companies and R&D-intensive industries like tech and pharmaceuticals. Shareholders capture most of the direct benefit; any broader gains depend on corporate behavior the bill cannot guarantee.

The new Retirement Savings, Lifetime Savings, and Lifetime Skills Accounts must be held as trusts administered by banks or approved trustees, making financial firms the required channel for these tax-advantaged savings vehicles and earning them administrative fees.

industries.industry: Investment funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The inflation-indexing provision extends basis adjustments to mutual funds and REITs and passes them through to their investors, reducing taxable gains for fund shareholders.
